newsitem.title: USA: US thrift regulator issues online banking guidance.
newsitem.headline: US thrift regulator issues online banking guidance.

text.p: U.S. savings and loans should develop risk-management strategies before offering electronic or online banking, Office of Thrift Supervision said in guidelines issued on Monday.
Security should be the paramount concern, the agency said, since online systems could in theory be used to break into a bank's electronic systems.
"Access via dial-up telephone and the Internet both represent an opening of the computer system to outside and potentially unauthorized users," the agency said.

Security controls that could be used to prevent unauthorized access include use of passwords or personal identification numbers, authentication software using digital certificates, encryption, and firewalls that create a security barrier separating various computer networks used by a bank, it said.

Online banking systems should be continuously tested to guard against vulnerabilities cropping up after a system is put in place, the agency said. "Outside hackers, disgruntled employees and inadvertent errors can adversely affect system reliability," the agency said.
"PC banking involves an open and dynamic environment that requires continuous testing and monitoring," the office said.

The eight-page guidance will be used by the agency's examiners when reviewing thrifts engaging in online banking. The outline also covers risks arising from outsourcing arrangements, technological developments, legal uncertainties and computer operations.
Thrifts are still be required to keep the regulator informed of planned online banking activity on a case-by-case basis.

The agency also said it was still assessing comment letters it received about whether any new rules are needed on electronic banking, smart cards and related issues. Proposed rules, if any, could be issued in the fall, the agency said.
